blocks.x: Arguably, the biggest challenge that Avengers: Doomsday presents for the Russo Brothers is finding screen time for the entire roster of Marvel Comics' superheroes across both the MCU and the 20th Century Fox era. Of course, that pales in comparison to the headache that would have accompanied the inclusion of the 80,000+ characters that are peppered throughout the long history of Marvel's comic books.

Not that anyone's complaining: the lineup as it stands, a healthy cross-section of heroes both well-known and, at least at one point in time, obscure (we're looking at you, Guardians of the Galaxy) is still enough to make us nerds of the world drool. Still, there are a number of Marvel heroes who are deserving of the big screen, and if not for the upcoming Avengers: Secret Wars, then at least in Phase 7 of the MCU. Here are the ten that should be at the top of the list, in no particular order.

blocks.c: Howard the Duck smashes through a newspaper.

blocks.x: Wait, wasn't there already a Howard the Duck movie? Why yes, yes there was. And it sucked. For that reason alone, the cynical, short-tempered anthropomorphic duck deserves another shot. Plus, his cameos in the Guardian of the Galaxy movies and Marvel's What If...? series were well-received, teasing a potential future in the MCU that has yet to manifest. Just make it happen, Kevin Feige.

Everyone knows Wolverine as a member of the X-Men, but his roots lie north of Lake Ontario in the Great White North, Canada, and superhero team Alpha Flight. Overseen by the Canadian military and answering directly to the Canadian Prime Minister, Alpha Flight is, for all intents and purposes, the Canadian Avengers. Founded by scientist James Hudson (who, along with his wife Heather, found Wolverine in the wild after the Weapon X program and nursed him back to health), the team consisted of Wolverine; Hudson, whose exosuit gave him powers as Guardian; twin mutants Jean-Paul and Jeanne-Marie Beaubier, known respectively as Northstar and Aurora, with powers of super-speed and light generation; Walter Langkowski, aka the giant fur-covered Hulk-like beast Sasquatch; First Nations medicine man Michael Twoyoungmen, aka Shaman; and Snowbird, an Inuk demi-goddess.

Their ties to the very popular Wolverine are well-documented, and with the X-Men poised to center the MCU's Phase 7, it certainly wouldn't be difficult to bring in Alpha Flight. Like Captain Britain, it adds an international element, albeit much closer to home, that would be a welcome element. And they'd certainly be much more polite.

blocks.c: Squirrel Girl as seen in Marvel Rivals.

blocks.x: Canadian Doreen Green learned that she could communicate with squirrels at the age of 10, along with other squirrel-like abilities and a prehensile tail, the result of an unknown modification in her genes (but not a mutant). In her first appearance in 1991, Doreen, now 14, finds Iron Man in a forest and works hard to convince him that she should be his sidekick. Her and her pet squirrel Monkey Joe, that is. Doreen makes a solid case for it by rescuing Iron Man from Doctor Doom (!) with the help of a horde of squirrels (which she would also use to take out Maelstrom later on). He still declines her request, but does offer to put in a good word for her to the Avengers when she's older. Years later, now living in New York City, Squirrel Girl joins the Great Lakes Avengers, and the rest, as they say, is history.

Squirrel Girl is a fun, fun character and deceptively powerful in her own right (did we mention she took out Doctor Doom?), and she's already been tossed around as a possible addition to the MCU, with Anna Kendrick attached to the role. And if the Great Lakes Avengers does become a thing as hoped, then BOOM. Done. But why should I convince you of Squirrel Girl's awesomeness when Collider already has?

blocks.c: Captain Britain, with the Union Jack behind.

blocks.x: Captain Britain was created as an exclusive British character to serve as the flagship title of Marvel UK, debuting in the pages of Captain Britain #1 in October 1976, and while three people have held the title, the name most commonly associated with the character is also the first: Brian Braddock. Hailing from the town of Maldon in Essex, Brian left his home after the loss of his parents (believed to be due to a lab accident before later revealed as murder) to study at the Thames University in London. He also spent downtime working at the Darkmoor Nuclear Research Facility, which unfortunately timed with it being attacked by the Reaver. Brian escaped and tried to get help, but the Reaver ran his motorcycle off the road and down a cliff.

Brian lay fatally wounded, but was woken by Merlyn, the magician, and his daughter, Roma. They offered him the chance to save his life by selecting either the Amulet of Right or the Sword of Might. Brian chose the amulet, transforming into Captain Britain and defeating the Reaver. From that point on, whenever needed, all Brian had to do was touch the amulet and become Captain Britain. The character has a strong connection with the X-Men, given his twin sister Betsy, who also held the mantle of Captain Britain, is on the team of mutants as Psylocke, so it would be an easy progression in Phase 7. It would also give the MCU an international element that is largely missing.

blocks.c: Nova (aka Richard Rider) stands in space.
